what_it_does: Many important computations — such as graph analysis (like finding shortest paths or ranking web pages) and scientific simulations on sparse matrices (large tables where most entries are zero and only a few matter) — have highly irregular, unpredictable memory access patterns that cause fixed-purpose AI accelerator chips to perform poorly, because those chips assume data arrives in neat, regular patterns. Quartz is a chip designed specifically for these unpredictable 'sparse' workloads, with two key architectural ideas: its processing elements and its on-chip fast memory banks (collections of small, quick storage blocks spread across the chip rather than in one central location) are connected through a re-programmable routing network, so the path data takes through the chip can be reconfigured at runtime to match whatever a given sparse computation requires. The distributed layout of the memory banks also means many memory requests can be served simultaneously from different banks, avoiding the traffic jam that occurs when all requests funnel through a central memory.
